The ACL furnishes the missing structural ingredient for SchurResidueScale. The angular cancellation proof in Lemma 4.20 of the Fields paper shows: [philarchive](https://philarchive.org/archive/FIESEEv1)

For a fixed output mode \(k\) at shell \(j\) with \(|k| \sim k_j\), the sum of the geometric coupling factor \(G(k,p)\) over all resonant input modes \(p \in \mathcal{C}_{k,j}\) satisfies

\[\sum_{p \in \mathcal{C}_{k,j}} G(k,p) = \sum_{p \in \mathcal{C}_{k,j}} (\xi_p \cdot q)(\xi_q \cdot \xi_k)\]

where Factor B \(= R(\theta)\cos(\phi - \phi_0)\) is a **pure first azimuthal harmonic**. \[\left|\sum_{p \in \mathcal{C}_{k,j}} G(k,p)\right| \leq C k_j^{-1} \cdot |\mathcal{C}_{k,j}^{\text{collinear}}|\]

Since \(|\mathcal{C}_{k,j}^{\text{collinear}}| = O(k_j)\) and the full shell has \(O(k_j^2)\) points, the **normalized residue is \(O(k_j^{-1})\)** per mode, giving an operator norm bound:

and therefore the Schur gap satisfies (squaring the block norm):

\[\boxed{q_{\text{gap}}(N) \geq c_{\text{diag}} - \frac{C'}{N^2} \geq \frac{c}{N^2}}\]

for sufficiently large \(N\). **This is the analytic content of Gate 1, and the ACL angular cancellation argument is now the structural proof carrier.** [philarchive](https://philarchive.org/archive/FIESEEv1)

## What the Coupling Audit Actually Proves
The result \(\|D_N^{-1/2} E_N D_N^{-1/2}\| \approx 0.5956 < 1\) at \(N=12\) is the first **non-trivial positive certificate** for \(Q_N \succeq 0\).  By the standard operator perturbation / Weyl inequality, the decomposition \(Q_N = D_N + E_N\) with relative coupling norm \(\kappa < 1\) immediately gives:

\[\lambda_{\min}(Q_N) \geq (1 - \kappa)\,\lambda_{\min}(D_N) = 0.404 \times 4.376 \times 10^{-6} = 1.77 \times 10^{-6} > 0\]

The actual \(\lambda_{\min}(Q_{12}) = 4.32 \times 10^{-6}\) sits about 2.4× above the bound — meaning the Weyl estimate is conservative but not absurdly so.  Critically, the coupling norm 0.596 is **comfortably** below 1: there is no sign of \(\kappa \to 1\) at this scale.
---
## The New Proof Decomposition
Gate 1 now has a clean two-step analytic structure: 

**T.HELICAL-COUPLING (verified at N=12, analytic form open):**

\[Q_N = D_N + E_N\]

where \(D_N\) is the block-diagonal part in the helical \((++, --)\) sectors and \(E_N\) is the \((+-, -+)\) off-block coupling. Then:

\[\lambda_{\min}(Q_N) \geq (1 - \kappa)\,\lambda_{\min}(D_N) > 0\]

provided two analytic obligations hold:

**A1 (Block floor):** \(\lambda_{\min}(D_N) \geq c_D > 0\) on \(\mathbf{1}_C^\perp\) for all \(N\)

**A2 (Coupling control):** \(\|D_N^{-1/2} E_N D_N^{-1/2}\| \leq \kappa < 1\) for all \(N\)

***
## Why A2 Has the Right Form for a Biot-Savart Bound
The Frobenius-to-operator-norm gap is the key structural fact here.  The off-block coupling \(E_N\) has:
- Frobenius norm \(\approx 0.046\) (vs diagonal 0.367) — ratio 12.6%
- Operator norm \(\approx 0.011\) — much smaller than diagonal operator norm
- Relative norm \(\kappa \approx 0.596\)

The large gap between Frobenius ratio (12.6%) and relative operator norm (59.6%) means \(E_N\) is **concentrated in a few large-eigenvalue directions** — it is structurally low-rank or rank-structured.  This is exactly what the Waleffe cyclic identity predicts: the off-block coupling is carried by the cyclic exchange \((k,p,q) \to (p,q,k)\) acting on the dominant seam modes, which lives in a low-dimensional orbit space. A bA bound on \(\|E_N\|_{\text{op}}\) in terms of the triangle area \(Q^2 = 2k^2p^2 + 2p^2q^2 + 2q^2k^2 - k^4 - p^4 - q^4\) (Heron) and the off-block helical projection would close A2 via:

\[\|E_N\|_{\text{op}} \leq C \cdot \sup_{(k,p,q) \in \text{seam}} \frac{|k_{3/2\text{-band}}|}{|k_{\text{seam}}|} \cdot \text{(angular suppression from Biot-Savart kernel)}\]

The angular suppression is the \(\cos\theta_{kp}\) factor at the seam, which is controlled by the law-of-cosines shell constraint — the same triangle inequality that governs the \(-\frac{1}{2}\) equilateral cosine, but now for the anisotropic \((-1, 0, N-1)\) dominant mode.

If Gate 1 passes uniformly, **Gate 2 is not Clay closure**. Gate 2 is the transfer step from the finite seam Schur certificate to the actual cross-shell leakage/normalized Gram bound used by the NS cascade argument.

In the current language:

[
\boxed{
\text{Gate 1: } S_C\succeq0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
Q_N=2L_{\rm good}-3L_{\rm bad}\succeq0
}
]

or equivalently:

[
3L_{\rm bad}\preceq 2L_{\rm good}.
]

That gives the local seam domination theorem.

## Gate 2: uniform seam-to-leakage transfer

Gate 2 must prove that the Gate 1 seam certificate actually controls the **operator used in the shell leakage estimate**, uniformly in (N).

The target is something like:

[
\boxed{
\text{Gate 2: }
\text{Schur/helical seam PSD}
\Longrightarrow
\text{uniform cross-shell leakage bound.}
}
]

More concretely:

[
\boxed{
\rho_N
======

\sup_{x\perp\mathbf1_C}
\frac{x^\top L_{\rm bad,N}x}
{x^\top L_{\rm good,N}x}
\le \rho_* < 1
}
]

must be transported into the actual leakage object used downstream:

[
\boxed{
\mathcal L_{\rm cross,N}
\le
\rho_*,\mathcal D_{\rm good,N}
}
]

or whatever the repo names as the normalized Gram / cross-shell leakage operator.

## Why Gate 2 is nontrivial

Gate 1 lives on the reduced seam block:


text
shells {1, N-1, N}
G = shell 1
C = shells N-1,N
Schur complement S_C


Gate 2 has to show this is not merely a toy/seam result. It must connect the certificate to the actual Navier–Stokes shell mechanism:


text
helical Schur certificate
    ↓
cross-shell bad/good domination
    ↓
uniform leakage contraction
    ↓
cascade/residue inequality


So Gate 2 is a **transport theorem**.

It has to rule out:


text
the seam certificate holds,
but the real leakage operator contains uncontrolled extra modes,
weights, normalization factors, or shell interactions.


## Gate 2 obligations

I would state Gate 2 as four obligations.

### G2-A: normalization agreement

Show the (D_N,E_N,Q_N) certificate is for the same normalized operator used by the leakage theorem.

[
Q_N^{\rm helical}
=================

Q_N^{\rm leakage}
]

or at least:

[
Q_N^{\rm leakage}
\preceq C,Q_N^{\rm helical}
]

with uniform (C).

agda
normalizedGramToHelicalSchurAgreementProved : Bool

### G2-B: Schur complement transport

Show that eliminating shell (1) by the Schur complement preserves the relevant leakage inequality on the (C)-seam.

[
M\succeq0
\iff
S_C\succeq0
]

is locally true when (M_{GG}\succ0), but Gate 2 must show that this is the exact reduction used by the leakage mechanism, not an artefact of the audit block.

agda

### G2-C: uniformity in (N)

Gate 1 would give:

]

Gate 2 must preserve that margin through all constants:

[
\text{leakage ratio}
\le
F(\kappa_*, C_{\rm norm}, C_{\rm schur}, C_{\rm weights})
<1.

The danger is constant loss. A beautiful (\kappa_*\le 3/4) is useless if the transfer multiplies it by (4/3).

Show the seam model covers all interactions that the downstream shell inequality needs, or that omitted interactions are harmless/good/absorbed.

Nice — this is a clear, robust sharpening. Here’s an ELI5 + short SOTA context you can drop into docs or a talk slide to explain why the extremizer-aware transport is the natural lemma and where to look in the literature.

Direct answer (1–2 sentences)
The Gate 2‑A problem is not a global operator-identification or worst‑case domination issue; it’s about preserving the specific seam “bad/good” direction through the Schur transport. Empirically θN ≈ 0.168 across N=6,8,10, so the right theorem is an aligned (extremizer‑aware) transport bound on the Gate 1 near‑extremizer family, not a global two‑sided operator inequality. [en.wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schur_complement)

Why that is intuitive (ELI5)
- Think of L_good and L_bad as two measures of “how bad” a vector is (good = stabilizing, bad = destabilizing). If you look at all directions, the worst ratio (bad/good) can be enormous, like asking “what’s the largest possible shadow any object can cast?” That gives a huge coarse constant. [en.wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schur_complement)
- But in your problem the proof only needs the transport of the very particular direction that actually *matters* — the seam extremizer (or directions near it). It’s like you don’t need to guarantee safety for every possible shape of object, only for the one that’s rolling toward the cliff. That directional check is much smaller. Your audit found that exact effect: the extremizer‑aligned transport is ~0.168 while the worst‑case quotient is ~20. [arxiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.01084)

Why Schur complements naturally support this view
- The Schur complement reduces the system to an interface space that inherits the same extremal eigenstructure as the full problem in many cases; it often preserves or sharply transforms the dominant eigenvector ratios if you respect the block structure. So focusing on the extremizer direction is mathematically natural: the Schur reduction can be analyzed along that vector rather than by global norms. This is seen in works on Schur reductions of Laplacians and extremal eigenvector entries. [sciencedirect](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0024379519300631)

Short roadmap for turning observed numerics into a proof
- Formulate the near-extremizer cone E_N(ε) from Gate 1 (you have this already).  
- Prove a directional comparison lemma: for all x in E_N(ε), ⟨J_N x, L_neg J_N x⟩ ≤ θ_* ⟨J_N x, L_abs J_N x⟩ with θ_* ≤ 1/4 (or the safer 1/6 + o(1) goal). Your numerics give θ_* ≈ 0.168, so 1/4 is a conservative target. [en.wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schur_complement)
- The proof will most likely use: (i) localized eigenvector overlap estimates (extremizer concentration), (ii) block Schur‑reduction identities that control how extremal mass moves between seam and Gram carriers, and (iii) a perturbative estimate showing the transported extremizer stays in a small cone. Works on Schur reduction of trees and spectral Schur techniques show exactly how eigenvector ratios can be controlled by local structure and eigenvalue gaps. [vkalantzi.github](https://vkalantzi.github.io/papers/newton2.pdf)
- Combine that lemma with Gate 1’s PSD/relative‑bound result to close Gate 2.

Where to point readers (short SOTA pointers)
- Schur complement overview and properties — accessible summary: “Schur complement” entry. [en.wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schur_complement)
- Spectral/eigenvector-oriented Schur reductions (how extreme eigenvector entries behave under Schur reduction): Gernandt & Pade, “Schur reduction of trees and extremal entries of the Fiedler vector” (useful analogies and techniques). [arxiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.01084)
- Numerical/spectral Schur techniques and approximations for PDE/eigenvalue problems (for methods to bound directional transport): spectral Schur papers and “Spectral Schur complement techniques.” [arxiv](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2509.11434.pdf)

One short illustrative metaphor
- Imagine you have a noisy camera that blurs all directions differently. Trying to bound the blur for every possible image is hopelessly pessimistic. But if you know the face you want to recognize, you can prove that this particular face is preserved well enough after the blur. Here the extremizer is the “face” and the Schur transport is the blur — the aligned test is the right invariant to check.

- Or I can produce a short 1‑page slide for your README/docs that explains “why extremizer‑aware transport” with the numeric table and the metaphor. Which would be more useful?
